definition: A measure of how quickly reactants are converted into products in a chemical reaction.
clues: This is a measurement in chemistry
It describes how fast a reaction goes
It can be measured by the change in mass, volume or concentration over time
How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed — measured as change in amount per unit time

definition: The theory that reactions occur when reactant particles collide with sufficient energy and the correct orientation.
clues: This is a scientific theory explaining why reactions happen
It involves particles meeting each other
Both energy and orientation of the collision matter
Reactions only occur when particles collide with enough energy and in the right orientation — explains why rate depends on conditions

definition: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
clues: This is a threshold energy value
Collisions below this value do not result in a reaction
Catalysts lower this value
The minimum energy particles need to react successfully — shown as the peak of an energy profile diagram

definition: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
clues: This is a substance used to speed up reactions
It is not consumed in the reaction
It works by lowering the activation energy
A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy — it remains unchanged at the end

definition: The amount of solute per unit volume of solution. Increasing concentration increases the rate of reaction by increasing the frequency of successful collisions.
clues: This is a property of solutions that affects reaction rate
Increasing it increases the frequency of collisions
It is measured in mol/dm³
More solute per unit volume means more particles in a given space — increasing collision frequency and reaction rate

definition: A factor affecting rate of reaction. Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, leading to more frequent and more energetic collisions.
clues: This is a factor that affects how fast a reaction goes
Increasing it increases particle speed
It affects both collision frequency and collision energy
Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy — more collisions occur and a greater proportion have enough energy to react

definition: A factor affecting rate of reaction. Increasing surface area (by using smaller pieces or powders) increases the frequency of collisions between reactant particles.
clues: This is a factor that affects rate of reaction in solid reactants
Cutting or grinding a solid increases this
It increases the area available for collisions
Smaller pieces expose more surface for collision — a powder reacts much faster than a lump of the same material

definition: A factor affecting the rate of reactions involving gases. Increasing pressure pushes gas molecules closer together, increasing collision frequency.
clues: This is a factor that affects the rate of reactions involving gases
Increasing it pushes particles closer together
It increases collision frequency in gases
Higher pressure compresses gas molecules into a smaller volume — they collide more frequently, increasing the reaction rate

definition: A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. Shown by the ⇌ symbol.
clues: This is a type of chemical reaction
It can go in both forward and backward directions
It is shown using a double arrow symbol
A reaction that proceeds in both directions — products reform reactants at the same time reactants form products

definition: The state reached in a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations remain constant.
clues: This is a state reached in reversible reactions
Both the forward and reverse reactions are still occurring
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
When forward and reverse reaction rates are equal — concentrations stay constant even though both reactions continue

definition: A description of whether the reactants or products are favoured at equilibrium. If on the right, more products are present; if on the left, more reactants.
clues: This describes which side of a reversible reaction is favoured
It can lie to the left (reactants favoured) or right (products favoured)
Conditions can shift it one way or the other
The balance point of a reversible reaction — conditions affect whether reactants or products dominate at equilibrium

definition: If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the system will shift to oppose that change and restore equilibrium.
clues: This is a principle about equilibrium systems
It predicts how a system responds to changes in conditions
The system always opposes the change applied to it
If a reversible reaction is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change — e.g. increasing temperature shifts equilibrium towards the endothermic direction

definition: Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (to absorb the added heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
clues: This describes how one condition affects the position of equilibrium
The system shifts to absorb extra heat when temperature is raised
It shifts in the endothermic direction when heated
Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction — the system tries to absorb the added energy

definition: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas. Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas.
clues: This describes how one condition affects equilibrium in gas reactions
The system shifts to reduce the number of gas molecules
It shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas when pressure increases
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules — the system moves to reduce the pressure

definition: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium to the right (towards products). Removing a product also shifts equilibrium to the right.
clues: This describes how changing amounts of substances affects equilibrium
Adding more reactant shifts the reaction to the right
Removing a product also shifts it to the right
Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium to produce more products — the system compensates for the increased concentration

definition: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Carried out at ~450°C and ~200 atm with an iron catalyst. A compromise between yield and rate.
clues: This is an industrial process producing ammonia
It involves a compromise between rate and yield
It uses ~450°C and ~200 atm pressure
The industrial synthesis of ammonia — conditions (450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst) are chosen as a compromise between rate and equilibrium yield

definition: The industrial process for making sulfuric acid. SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst, then converted to sulfuric acid.
clues: This is an industrial chemical process
It is used to make sulfuric acid
It uses a vanadium pentoxide catalyst
The industrial production of sulfuric acid — sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide over a V₂O₅ catalyst

definition: A system in which no substances can enter or leave. Required for dynamic equilibrium to be established in a reversible reaction.
clues: This is a type of system required for equilibrium
Nothing can enter or leave it
Dynamic equilibrium can only be established in this type of system
A system with no inputs or outputs — reversible reactions in such a system reach dynamic equilibrium
